title: Ringbrothers “Billie” Is a Big, Bad GTO with a Sweet Backstory

body_markdown:
Hot rod fans know at this point that[Ringbrothers](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/ringbrothers/) customs and the annual Specialty Equipment Market Association ([SEMA](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/sema/) ) show go together like peanut butter and jelly. If you follow the shop on Instagram, you’ve been briefed that this year’s build is a 1965 GTO named Billie. Now, we are pleased to share plenty of photos and all of the juicy details surrounding the 5500-hour build, which started life as a regular Tempest.


What we appreciate most about Wisconsin’s Ringbrothers is how well and how convincingly it can extensively modify a car’s body. Billie’s body is five inches wider than stock, but it looks nevertheless understated and natural. Minding scale is key, and the hood scoop on this car is a great example: Though it’s 20 percent bigger than the original, the proportions are the same.


“We spent countless hours massaging the factory lines,” says Jim Ring, “reshaping the fenders and refining how every panel transitions into the next.” Another example is the section of the rear that reads PONTIAC. Ringbrothers remachined the middle of that piece—the part that bears the letters—so that it (literally and aesthetically) fit the widened body.

That enlarged hood scoop sits on a hood made of carbon fiber—a material that also appears on the front wheel tubs, the doors, and the rear diffuser—and helps route air to a supercharged, 6.2-liter LT4 V-8. Built by Wegner Motorsports and backed by a 10-speed automatic from Bowler Performance, the powerplant is good for 650 hp and 650 lb-ft of torque. A set of HRE wheels wrapped in aggressive Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 tires hide Fox coilovers and six-piston Brembo brakes. The chassis is a Roadster Shop affair, a “Stage III” version of its Fast Track line. GTO aficionados will be quick to spot that the exhaust tips sit in the rear bumper rather than below the rear fenders, a visible concession to the car’s modernization that isn’t beyond the pale.


Ringbrothers / David Heller


Ringbrothers / David Heller

The interior is much the same story as the outside: The shapes and silhouettes ooze vintage charm, but subtly (and thoroughly) updated with modern componentry and materials, like Dakota Digital instruments and gray and blue leather. What you might not notice, unless you’re intimately familiar with these cars, is where that dashboard sits: It’s been moved four inches forward and two inches lower. Like the outside, the interior gleams with machined aluminum and is studded with custom emblems.

Want in-progress photos? Ringbrothers has got you covered.


Having enjoyed many years at the top of their game, the Ringbrothers enjoy the luxury of discernment when it comes to selecting projects, and the story behind this commission is especially touching. “Billie began as a tribute to a GTO once owned by our client’s mother, who received the original car as a gift,” says Mike Ring. “The owner wanted to recreate something that held real sentimental value, and during our early conversations, he suggested calling it “Goat.” We came back with Billie, as in billy goat, and that moniker stuck. It’s a playful nod to the GTO’s heritage, but more, a deeply personal tribute to a car with a special place in his family’s history.”


Stay tuned for more news[from the SEMA show floor](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/sema-2026/) later this week, as our own hot rod expert[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/) brings us the most interesting stories from this annual celebration of all things aftermarket.
